To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
prolonged visual exposure to a stimulus produces an adaptation aftereffect that occurs not only for low-level properties (e.g. faces’ gender) but also for high level properties (e.g bodies’ gender).
prolonged exposure to a face (either frontal view or silhouette face profiles) produces a perceptual aftereffect in body gender perception.
adaptation to both female and male faces produces gender aftereffect in body perception.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the cross-categorical adaptation and provides a better understanding of the relationship between body and face perception.
the perceptual adaptation between cross-category stimuli and the aftereffects that occur in the perception of the human body.
the role of semantic information in perceptual adaptation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
cross-category adaptation can be induced between two stimuli that share common semantic properties, and that this effect is not restricted to the physical properties of the stimuli.
the cross-category adaptation is not a simple aftereffect but a more complex phenomenon that involves a variety of mechanisms.
adaptation to faces produces gender adaptation aftereffects in body perceptions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the adaptation aftereffects can be induced by the shared semantic attributes, rather than physical properties, of the adapters and the test stimuli.
the aftereffect can occur in the high-level category of human bodies, which is a cross-category of faces.
adaptation to face profiles can produce aftereffects for the perception of bodies.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the aftereffect can occur not only for simple physical features but also for semantic features.
the adaptation effect is not limited to the physical property (i.e. gender) of the adapter but to the common properties (i.e. the semantic attribute of gender) shared by the adapters and the test.
the aftereffect can be used to study the semantic attributes shared by two different stimulus categories.
